title: Count divisors by making independent choices
chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
goal: Count the factors of a number by choosing how many of each prime to use.

scenes.visual: Build factor pairs for twelve and sort their six distinct entries.
scenes.narration: Twelve has six positive factors: one, two, three, four, six and twelve. We can list those by finding the products that make twelve. For a larger number, it is easier to count choices from its prime factorisation.

scenes.visual: Show the prime powers of 360 and preview the three independent counts.
scenes.narration: Three hundred and sixty factorises into two cubed, three squared and five. Its full factor list has twenty-four entries. We can account for them through three small counts, one for each prime. Let's see how this works with twelve first.

scenes.visual: Show twelve made from two twos and one three. Hold the question of all distinct possible products.
scenes.narration: Twelve is two times two times three. A factor of twelve is made from some of those prime tiles. Think about how many twos you can use. Then think about your choices for the three. How many different products are possible?

scenes.visual: Fill a three by two grid using independent prime counts, including the empty choice.
scenes.narration: Use zero, one or two twos. That gives three choices. For each of them, either include the three or leave it out. That gives two choices. Three times two makes six products. Taking no tiles gives one. Taking all the tiles gives twelve. Every cell makes a different factor.

scenes.visual: Build a four by three grid for the powers in 72. Show the count and return briefly to 360.
scenes.narration: Seventy-two is two cubed times three squared. Choose zero, one, two or three twos. For each choice there are three possibilities for the threes. Four times three gives twelve factors. For three hundred and sixty, the extra choice about the five doubles that count to twenty-four.

scenes.visual: Pair the factors of thirty-six and centre the self-paired six. Use a shaded square to show why it has a single middle factor.
scenes.narration: For thirty-six, the factor pairs are one and thirty-six, two and eighteen, three and twelve, and four and nine. Six pairs with itself, so it appears just once in the list. A factor pairs with itself exactly when its square is the number. That is why square numbers have an odd count of positive factors.

scenes.visual: Show the exponent-plus-one rule and an unfilled factor count for two hundred.
scenes.narration: For each prime, include the choice to use zero copies. Add one to the prime's exponent, and multiply the resulting counts. In your notebook, find the number of positive factors of two hundred, then explain why your method counts each factor once.

notebook_exercise: How many positive factors does 200 have?
notebook_answer: 200 = 2³ × 5². Choose 0–3 twos and 0–2 fives, giving 4 × 3 = 12 factors.
